terms.vertical slice: A small experiment that carries one job the whole way down: something an agent does, the rule that guards it, and the way its data is kept.
terms.slate: The ordered list of vertical slices that the review proposes.
terms.world: An agent's own version of the data. It sees its own changes and nobody else's until it lands.
terms.landing: Applying a world's calls to the shared data, all of them or none.
terms.view: A function that narrows which data an agent may read or change.
terms.read program: A small program or function an agent writes to read the data, in place of a fixed query.
terms.Mo: The language and runtime the database is written in. A Mo service keeps its whole state in memory and saves the whole state on every write.

state.review:
I recommend four slices, each extending the same small job. These are proposed experiments, not database implementation. Before each run, freeze predictions, expected answers, workload bounds and a control that must fail. A failed result should narrow the candidate or trigger one targeted follow-up before proceeding.

1. Ask, decide, land.

An agent asks an unplanned question through a restricted view, then proposes approved calls in its world. Use a small, representative extract of the owner’s data, expressed as ordinary Mo records and collections.

Guard: read programs only compute; every answer is recorded; landing replays questions in their original positions, checks the rule after each call, and publishes the whole world atomically. Keep data in the existing numbered-node collection.

Experiment: test point reads, absence, aggregates, an intervening own write, and a concurrent change that alters underlying data while preserving the answer. Include a small agent exercise with answers written independently beforehand.

Required result: does this job work with correct answers and landings without widening the view or adding an operation for every question? Removing answer validation must admit a deliberately stale decision.

Mo today: use separately compiled read functions over exported snapshots; [the reference, §13.4](mo/docs/reference/README.md) documents offline queries. Live submission remains modelled: [design-ideas.md, “The request is a program”](modb/design-ideas.md) identifies accepting programs while running as missing. The existing [worlds.mo, ask and land](modb/sketches/kept-versions/worlds.mo) records only keyed integer answers.

2. Authority changes while an agent thinks.

An agent delegates a narrower task; a person withdraws its grant or replaces an approved function before landing.

Guard: explicitly model which current authority must authorize each replayed call and release. Keep grant ancestry, approval identities, program versions and world roots as data beside the proposed changes.

Required result: can revocation prevent every subsequent unauthorized landing and release while unrelated authorized work still succeeds? The control checks authority only when the world opens and must wrongly accept withdrawn work.

Mo today: model the protocol; do not claim caller separation from a simulated caller identifier. [Design-ideas.md, “Many agents working together”](modb/design-ideas.md) names caller identity and derived grants as needs. [The reference, §11.5](mo/docs/reference/README.md) prohibits capabilities and functions in service state, inputs and results, so store identifiers rather than executable grants.

3. Lose the reply, recover the accountable change.

An agent lands, loses its connection, retries, and later asks what happened—even after an approved function changes.

Guard: one durable outcome binds request identity, caller, approval, questions, calls and relevant code version. Model an append record plus published root, with failures between every persistence step.

Required result: does recovery produce a complete accountable landing or none, with retries unable to repeat its effect? Include historical replay under the original definition. Publishing success before durability must fail the control.

Mo today: ordinary service recovery is a baseline, not this experiment’s proof. [The reference, §12.5](mo/docs/reference/README.md) says generated crashes occur between steps, never inside commits. [Saved-state.md, “Ownership and transactions”](mo/docs/design/saved-state.md) documents uncertain commit outcomes, absent request deduplication, unlogged successful reads and snapshot deletion of covered recovery logs. Model these stronger requirements without changing Mo.

4. Keep working, then forget abandoned worlds.

Run the same job repeatedly with fast and slow agents, abandoned worlds, retained history and increasing data sizes.

Guard: reclaim only unreachable versions; preserve every retained answer and approved landing. Compare today’s numbered-node representation with a model of fetching immutable nodes by identifier.

Required result: does a declared retention policy keep space and work within the chosen workload budget, including retries and slow-agent completion? Disabling reclamation must breach the budget; reclaiming a pinned version must corrupt a checked answer.

Mo today: [issue 37, “Not shown”](modb/issues/37-can-a-mo-library-keep-old-versions-cheaply-today.md) leaves reclamation and service-hosted worlds untested. Measure against MO_LIMIT_SERVICE_WORK, MO_LIMIT_SERVICE_MESSAGE_MEMORY and MO_LIMIT_SAVED_NODES in [limits.h](mo/src/base/limits.h). Paging needs modelling because service handlers cannot receive storage capabilities (§11.5); whole-state copying remains in [service.c, encoded_copy](mo/src/vm/service.c).

Run slice 1 first. It tests the distinctive agent experience and whether useful questions produce a tractable replay record. Cheap roots alone cannot answer that.

Stop when the evidence supports all five fields in [map.md, “Destination”](modb/map.md): database kind and novelty, borrowed ideas and costs, first real-data job, general Mo capabilities required, and relationship to Phases 6–8. Failures count if the decision explicitly excludes the failed promise. Continue only for an uncertainty that could reverse that decision.

I deliberately omit distribution, optimizers, framework packaging and general information-flow proofs. None is necessary to decide this bounded candidate. Retention experiments must not become claims of complete personal-data erasure.

The largest risk is separately successful slices hiding incompatible assumptions. Reuse one recorded scenario across all four, including authority changes, recovery and retention.

Confidence in slice 1 first: 80%. I would move recovery first if losing an answer makes the selected real-data job unacceptable even experimentally.

I read the specified snapshot and inspected Mo sources; I ran no experiments, independently reproduced no timings, and changed no files.

state.review:
I've read the snapshot and the Mo docs it depends on. I didn't run anything.

**The finding that most shapes my slate.** No file in the snapshot mentions `mo query`. design-ideas.md idea 1 calls the upgrade path "the nearest thing Mo has" to accepting a program. In fact Mo already runs a caller's own function over an exported state: `docs/agent-guide.md`, the `mo query` section, with export available through the `mo-export` MCP tool. It has a work limit (`MO_LIMIT_QUERY_WORK`, 2^30 instructions, in `src/base/limits.h`) and refuses capabilities or functions in parameters (E1411). It runs offline, not inside a live service. A call to a service gets only `MO_LIMIT_SERVICE_WORK`, 2^20 instructions, about a thousandth of that.

**1. Slate, in order**

**S1: questions asked again at landing.**
- **Agent does:** inside a world, runs two or three real read programs (a sum, a filter, a count by group) instead of the key lookups in `worlds.mo` `ask`. Each program's name, arguments and answer are recorded, and `land` runs them again on the main line.
- **Guard:** "every question counts, by its answer." Control: a world whose relied-on total changed must be sent back.
- **Data kept:** the tree by number (`tree.mo`).
- **Result, either way:** does re-running the recorded programs fit inside one landing call at 1k, 10k and 50k rows? The prediction gives the largest size at which it fits. Also measure the same programs through `mo query` on an export.
- **Mo in the way:** the 2^20 instruction limit per call; reference §11.5 forbids function values in state, so the programs must be a fixed set of named functions (a stand-in); new code arrives only by whole-service upgrade (`src/tools/protocol-upgrade.c`).

**S2: two real agents, one real dataset, through a running service.**
- **Agent does:** two model-driven agents work on the same data over MCP. Issue 12 must answer first which dataset.
- **Guard:** worlds land whole, with the rule checked after every call.
- **Data kept:** worlds as service state. Issue 37 "Not shown" says they have only run under `mo test`.
- **Result:** the needless send-back rate, the number design-ideas.md ("Which reads count as relied on") says the finer rule waits for. Prediction: above or below a threshold written in advance.
- **Mo in the way:** one token per service (`docs/design/services.md`), so callers are told apart only by an unauthenticated argument (a stand-in); `MO_LIMIT_MCP_RATE` of 20 calls a second; the 16 KiB request limit (I did not re-verify that number).

**S3: an agent proposes, a person approves, with a world open across it.**
- **Agent does:** proposes a new write function. It goes through the upgrade tools (`mo-upgrade-open/page/commit`) while another agent's world, recorded under the old code, is still open.
- **Guard:** "narrower is free, wider needs a person." Control: a widened view must not land without approval.
- **Result:** when the open world lands, does replaying it under the new code keep or break the replay rule? Either can happen.
- **Mo in the way:** upgrades replace the whole service; I did not check how a state migration interacts with the node map.

**S4: the kept log, and taking one agent's work out.**
- **Agent does:** every call carries a caller and a reason. Remove one agent's calls and replay what came after.
- **Guard:** the accountable write.
- **Data kept:** the log inside the state, because Mo deletes its own log at each snapshot, every 100 messages (`MO_LIMIT_SERVICE_SNAPSHOT_MESSAGES`).
- **Result:** the calls predicted to be refused or changed by the removal, against those actually found; and the log length at which the memory ceiling stops writes.
- **Mo in the way:** no caller identity; the log is not kept.

**S5: write only what changed (a measurement or model, not a build).**
- **Result:** with only changed nodes written, does a write's cost become flat as the state grows?
- **Mo in the way:** `encoded_copy` in `src/vm/service.c` encodes the whole state; §11.5 forbids capabilities in a handler; files have no byte writes, seek or sync (map.md, "Mo on 2026-11-13"). So this can only be measured outside a service.

**2. Run S1 first.** "Every question counts, by its answer" is decided and is the newest idea here. Yet the only test of it, `worlds.mo`, uses single-key questions, which are nearly free to ask again. Read programs are what make it expensive, and landing runs inside the smallest work limit. If S1 fails at modest sizes, the decided rule needs another mechanism, such as answer 6 or re-checking outside the call. That would change S2 through S4. S1 also builds directly on existing code and needs nobody's data.

**3. Stop rule.** Write the decision when all three hold:
- (a) each of the map's five destination items cites at least one slice result. Item 3 must come from a slice on the owner's real data; every gap under item 4 must have been hit by a slice, not inferred from reading.
- (b) two slices in a row have added no new Mo gap and have not changed the one-sentence statement of what is new (map.md "Not yet specified").
- (c) the library-or-runtime question for storage has a measured answer (S5).

If five slices run without meeting all three, write the decision anyway and list the gaps that are still open.

**4. Deliberately left out.**
- Sensitivity labels in types (idea 9): Mo has nothing for them, so they can't be sliced. They need a type-system design and Lean.
- Views kept current and indexes (ideas 8 and storage): left until S2 shows read programs are actually slow.
- Erasing data from history, and chains of helper grants: they need S4's log first.
- Fairness between fast and slow agents, and the 10 ms HTTP layer: the first is a later deep dive; the second is Mo's own matter.
- Batteries and memory safety: deferred and parked by the owner.

**5. Largest risk: stand-ins pile up until they become the design.** So far the slices have used:
- views written as key predicates;
- the rule written twice, as a promise and as `rule?`;
- a bare map in place of a record;
- named functions in place of submitted programs;
- self-declared callers.

Each slice passes on its own, and nobody runs them together. Guards:
- each slice extends the previous slice's code in one sketch, instead of starting fresh;
- a slice isn't done until its stand-ins are listed, each with what would replace it;
- the decision may only cite results whose stand-ins it names.

**6. Confidence that S1 should be first: about 65%.** I would change my mind if issue 12's answer names data that agents mostly append to and rarely re-read; S2 would then go first. I would also change it if one look at real agent transcripts shows their questions are nearly all single-key lookups, which would make S1's cost moot.

What I didn't check: I did not run the sketches or `mo query`, did not read `models/` or the council's raw files, and did not verify the 16 KiB request limit.

terms.vertical slice: A small experiment that carries one job the whole way down: something an agent does, the rule that guards it, and the way its data is kept.
terms.slate: The ordered list of vertical slices that the review proposes.
terms.world: An agent's own version of the data. It sees its own changes and nobody else's until it lands.
terms.landing: Applying a world's calls to the shared data, all of them or none.
terms.view: A function that narrows which data an agent may read or change.
terms.read program: A small program or function an agent writes to read the data, in place of a fixed query.
terms.Mo: The language and runtime the database is written in. A Mo service keeps its whole state in memory and saves the whole state on every write.

state.review:
1. SLATE (FOUR SLICES, IN ORDER)

Slice 1: Cold-agent read programs, narrowed views, and answer-checked landing.
Agent: Cold agents (given types, signatures, and examples) write pure Mo read functions over a narrowed View on issues/12-what-real-data-goes-in-first.md ("Candidate datasets") data, concurrently asking, calling writes, and landing (design-ideas.md, "1. The request is a program").
Guard/control: mo_check_query_entry (src/check/services.c) rejects effects/hidden fields; land replays reads in place (issues/35-what-lands-together-when-a-world-holds-more-than-one-call.md, "Answer") and checks rules per call. Control: expose hidden fields or skip replay; bad reads compile or races land.
Kept: sketches/kept-versions/tree.mo (put, keep, open) plus in-state log, queried via mo fetch (src/tools/fetch.c) and query (src/tools/offline.c).
Result: Cold agents pass a pre-set validity bar without SQL AND coarse-read send-backs (design-ideas.md, "Which reads count as relied on") stay below ceiling, OR one fails.
Mo blockers: Offline-only query (src/tools/offline.c); whole-service mo_live_start (src/tools/upgrade-live.c); mo_check_service_purity (src/check/services.c; docs/reference/README.md, "11.5 Purity") barring function values; struct-Map copy in borrow_walk (src/codegen/ownership.c; sketches/kept-versions/in-place.mo).

Slice 2: Delegated helper worlds, O(log N) checks, and selective undo on mo serve.
Agent: Over mo serve MCP, parents mint narrower grants (view, writes, call cap, Time expiry) for helpers, and an operator undoes one misled agent's calls by replay (design-ideas.md, "Many agents working together", "4. The log is the truth").
Guard/control: Helpers only narrow parent grants and die on revocation; rules read summaries instead of O(N) Tree.entries in sketches/kept-versions/worlds.mo (total); undo flags later calls with broken guards or changed answers. Control: omit narrowing or undo checks; escalation or drift lands.
Kept: service.sqlite (src/host/store.c) with tree.mo nodes, summaries, grants, and in-state call/read log.
Result: Delegation, O(log N) checks, and undo fit mo serve, OR hit MO_LIMIT_SERVICE_WORK (1,048,576), MO_LIMIT_MCP_RATE (20/s), 16/32 KiB MCP caps (src/base/limits.h), ~10 ms HTTP CPU (authenticate/plan, src/tools/protocol-request.c; issues/11-how-fast-and-large-is-a-mo-service.md, "Added later"), or 56 MiB call memory (mo_service_limits, src/vm/service.c).
Mo blockers: Single token (token_source, src/check/services.c; MO_LISTENER_AUTH, src/tools/protocol-request.c); no capabilities in state/messages (mo_check_service_purity); MO_STORE_SNAPSHOT (mo_store_call, src/host/store.c) deleting log; mo_service_step (src/vm/service.c) blocking reads behind writes.

Slice 3: Agent write/schema proposal, replay rehearsal, and human intent gate.
Agent: Blocked by a mid-world rule (issues/35-what-lands-together-when-a-world-holds-more-than-one-call.md, "Answer"), an agent proposes a composite write and migration, rehearses on Simulation and kept history, and submits an intent diff (design-ideas.md, "The ideas").
Guard/control: Must pass mo check --upgrade-from, mo test promises/recovery (src/tools/recovery.c), replay, and mo intent --against (src/tools/intent.c) gated on mo review (docs/agent-guide.md, "Review intent"). Control: push an unapproved or promise-weakening bundle; gate refuses.
Kept: service.sqlite via mo push --migrate (mo_live_admit, src/tools/upgrade-live.c) and program digests (src/host/store-programs.c).
Result: Phase 6 intent diffs and promises support human approval without duplicated rules, OR show test/runtime promise drift (sketches/land-whole/main.mo, rule? vs promise) and opaque diffs.
Mo blockers: Promises run only in mo test (src/tools/recovery.c), not mo_service_step (src/vm/service.c; docs/design/intent.md, "Service promises"); mo_live_admit ignores mo review (src/host/store-review.c); MO_LIMIT_UPGRADE_PREVIOUS=2 (src/base/limits.h); closed enum Call (sketches/README.md, "land-whole").

Slice 4: Path-only persistence, dead-world reclamation, and faulted-disk recovery versus service.sqlite.
Agent: Agents churn 90%-abandoned worlds and 10%-landed writes over 50k-500k records under sweeps and injected torn/lost writes (design-ideas.md, "Storage underneath"; issues/11-how-fast-and-large-is-a-mo-service.md, "Answer"; issues/37-can-a-mo-library-keep-old-versions-cheaply-today.md, "Not shown").
Guard/control: Recovery restores the last synced root with valid checksums, zero leaked nodes, and intact pinned roots. Control: write root before path sync or sweep live worlds; recovery or reads fail.
Kept: mo run sketch plus fault-injecting page/log harness writing dirty path nodes, beside yardstick.py and sketches/kept-versions/by-number.mo.
Result: Path-only writes and reclamation hold latency/memory near yardstick.py's ~3 ms floor, backing a custom engine, OR reclamation/hop costs favor fixing encoded_copy (src/vm/service.c) over service.sqlite.
Mo blockers: Files (src/base/hostops.def) lacks write_bytes, pread/pwrite, atomic rename, fsync; Files.in_memory and Simulation (docs/reference/README.md, "12.5 Simulation") inject no torn writes; src/base/prims.def lacks byte hash; services bar capabilities and force encoded_copy (MO_LIMIT_SAVED_BYTES 16 MiB, MO_LIMIT_SAVED_NODES 1,048,576, src/base/limits.h).

2. FIRST SLICE AND WHY
Run Slice 1 first. sketches/kept-versions/worlds.mo (ask, land) proved versioned trees in memory (issues/37-can-a-mo-library-keep-old-versions-cheaply-today.md, "Answer"), and TLA+ settled multi-call landing (issues/35-what-lands-together-when-a-world-holds-more-than-one-call.md, "Answer"). The sharpest untested bet is agent-facing: whether cold agents write pure Mo read functions over narrowed views without SQL, and whether answer-checked landing hits the 92-95% needless send-back rate in design-ideas.md ("What the first model and the research found"). (I listed mo/learnability/ folders without reading prompts; this snapshot has no DB query evals.) Failing either reshapes Slices 2-4.

3. STOP RULE
Stop once every map.md ("Destination", "Not yet specified") item has measured answers: query learnability and send-backs (Slice 1); multi-agent grants, O(log N) checks, and undo (Slice 2); human-gated proposals beside Phase 6 (Slice 3; issues/13-does-phase-6-finish-first.md, issues/18-how-does-it-sit-beside-phases-6-to-8.md); and saved-state versus custom storage plus general Mo additions passing issues/14-what-rule-keeps-the-database-from-bending-mo.md and issues/17-what-must-mo-gain.md (Slice 4)—stopping early if any core bet fails.

4. LEFT OUT AND WHY
Multi-machine replication (non-goal: design-ideas.md, "Open questions" #8); query optimizers/auto-indexes (premature before seeing agent read programs, unneeded at issues/12-what-real-data-goes-in-first.md scale); and re-testing HTTP parsing in src/tools/protocol-request.c (~10 ms CPU already isolated in issues/11-how-fast-and-large-is-a-mo-service.md, "Added later").

5. LARGEST SLICE RISK AND GUARD
Risk: toy-scale illusions where slices pass alone while hiding cross-slice breaks (O(N) rules in sketches/kept-versions/worlds.mo hitting MO_LIMIT_SERVICE_WORK at 1,000 inserts in issues/37-can-a-mo-library-keep-old-versions-cheaply-today.md, duplicated rules in sketches/land-whole/main.mo, or snapshot log deletion in src/host/store.c breaking undo). Guard: carry one issues/12-what-real-data-goes-in-first.md schema across all slices, pre-write numeric thresholds and controls, and vet each Mo ask against issues/14-what-rule-keeps-the-database-from-bending-mo.md.

6. CONFIDENCE IN FIRST SLICE
82%. I would run Slice 4 first if the chosen issues/12-what-real-data-goes-in-first.md dataset ("Candidate datasets") immediately exceeds encoded_copy's ~125,000-row / 16 MiB MO_LIMIT_SAVED_BYTES ceiling (issues/11-how-fast-and-large-is-a-mo-service.md, "Answer"), or if uninspected learnability/ runs already prove cold-agent Mo query fluency.

**Needs.** Telling callers apart. Grants for each caller, and grants made from grants. Worlds, which need the tree from the storage section. A record of what each world read. Running reads alongside the one writer.

evidence.text: **Decided by the owner on 2026-11-14: start simple and measure.** Every question counts, answers are compared, and the database counts needless send-backs. Landing whole worlds makes it sharper: a world with more calls has asked more questions, so more can change under it.

state.claim: The 16 MiB limit on saved state is what stops a service at about 125,000 rows.

evidence.text:
- At 100,000 rows the service reported 7,588,082 bytes of encoded state, 19.2 MB of heap in use and a peak of 51.3 MB. The limit for one call is 58,718,816 bytes: 64 MiB less the 8 MiB stack and less 1,440 bytes for the process record (`mo_process_new` in `src/vm/process.c`).
- At 125,000 rows it reported 9,488,082 bytes encoded (9.05 MiB) and a peak of 58,455,547 bytes. A write still worked. Adding 5,000 rows was refused three times with `memory_limit`: "the call ran out of memory; service state is unchanged".
- For small rows, then, the ceiling is the memory one call may use, reached at about 9 MiB of saved state. The 16 MiB limit on saved state is not what stops it. Each added row cost 76 bytes saved, 128 bytes of heap at rest and 287 bytes of heap at the peak of a write.

state.claim: Most of the time spent reading a request goes to the functions that authenticate it and plan it.

evidence.text:
*The fixed 10 ms of every call is the layer that reads the HTTP request.*

- Reads ran at the usual pace, 60 ms apart: 1,225 calls, none refused, 300 samples, 43 of them busy.
- 42 of the 43 were inside the VM (`mo_vm_execute`). 88% were under `mo_protocol_read`, which reads the request, and 9% under `mo_protocol_complete`.
- Handling the head of the request (`head_complete`) was in 72%: `authenticate` in 47% and `plan`, which decides what the request is, in 26%.
- What `authenticate` spends that time on is turning the request's headers into a Mo list of bytes and parsing them in Mo. The token itself is checked in C (`MO_LISTENER_AUTH`). `plan` then converts the headers a second time. A reviewer found both on 2026-11-14 (`src/tools/protocol-request.c`).
- That layer is Mo bytecode that the VM runs under a work budget. `authenticate` calls `mo_protocol_invoke(s, c, PF_INSPECT, args, &value)` (`src/tools/protocol-request.c`).
